articles.title: What is involuntary churn, and how do you measure it in Stripe?
articles.excerpt: Involuntary churn is the revenue you lose when a customer did not decide to leave. The card failed, nobody got them to fix it, and the subscription ended. You can measure it from Stripe data alone, bu…
articles.body: Involuntary churn is the revenue you lose when a customer did not decide to leave. The card failed, nobody got them to fix it, and the subscription ended. You can measure it from Stripe data alone, but only if you count it the same way every time. This article shows the counting rules I use, and where they can mislead you. What is involuntary churn? It is a cancellation that began with a failed payment, not with a decision. The customer still wanted the product. The card expired, hit its limit or was replaced, the renewal failed, and the follow-up either never came or came too late. Voluntary churn is the opposite: the customer chose to cancel. The two need different fixes. A failed card needs a card-update flow and well-timed retries.

articles.excerpt: I missed the HackerRank Orchestrate deadline, so I never submitted. I finished the project anyway, and this is what I built. Ghost Data Still Exists. A fictional company, Northstar Shop, lost $2.4M af…
articles.body: I missed the HackerRank Orchestrate deadline, so I never submitted. I finished the project anyway, and this is what I built. The challenge Ghost Data Still Exists . A fictional company, Northstar Shop, lost $2.4M after a "deleted" customer came back. Every dashboard said Complete, yet the email still couldn't re-register. The data was sitting in search indexes, support attachments, analytics exports, logs and backups. For each deletion request, the agent must say whether the data is really gone, and if not, what to do. The output is a status ( COMPLETE , INCOMPLETE or NOT_APPLICABLE ) plus ordered steps in three phases: finding, remediation, verification. I built and ran this on my local machine only. It isn't on GitHub. What I built and would defend 1. Negation gets checked first.

articles.title: Why your Galaxy battery drains faster after a firmware update, and what to do about it
articles.excerpt: A firmware update finishes, the phone reboots, and everything looks normal until you notice the battery percentage dropping far faster than it used to. It is one of the most common complaints after a…
articles.body: A firmware update finishes, the phone reboots, and everything looks normal until you notice the battery percentage dropping far faster than it used to. It is one of the most common complaints after a Samsung update, and it is also one of the most misunderstood. Sometimes the drain is temporary and fixes itself. Sometimes it points to a real problem the update exposed. Knowing which one you are dealing with saves you from wiping a phone that only needed a few days to settle. Why a new update uses more battery at first Right after an update, Android rebuilds a lot of things in the background. It re-indexes your files, re-optimises your apps for the new system version, and re-syncs accounts that were paused during the install.

articles.title: Five Signals That Tell You a GitHub Project Is Actually Alive
articles.excerpt: Every "best open source X" list has the same problem: half the projects are ghost ships. Last commit 2023, an issue queue of 900 unread, a README that still advertises a version two majors old. You fi…
articles.body: Every "best open source X" list has the same problem: half the projects are ghost ships. Last commit 2023, an issue queue of 900 unread, a README that still advertises a version two majors old. You find out after you've installed it. Here's the checklist I run now. It takes about five minutes per project and has saved me more time than any comparison article. 1. pushed_at , not the last release The release page lies. A project can cut a "v2.1.0" that's a version bump and nothing else, or ship nothing for a year while the repo is very much alive. What you want is the last commit to the default branch . In the GitHub API that's pushed_at . If it's within a couple of weeks, someone is in the code. If it's six months old, ask why before you install.

articles.title: A physics layer that draws nothing: reading interface forces back as CSS variables
articles.excerpt: Most interface physics runs one way. Something moves, and the page watches. I build Fundamental, a relational field runtime for interfaces. Elements bend a shared field, and the field bends them back.…
articles.body: Most interface physics runs one way. Something moves, and the page watches. I build Fundamental, a relational field runtime for interfaces. Elements bend a shared field, and the field bends them back. The second half is the part I care about. The field reports what it feels as live CSS variables, so the page can style itself from the result. Bodies A body is any element with a data-body attribute. Its value is one or more force tokens. <field-root render = "dots" ></field-root> <h1 data-body = "attract" data-strength = "1.2" data-feedback > Mass </h1> <button data-body = "repel" data-range = "240" > Keep clear </button> <field-root> goes on the page once. It finds every [data-body] element and wires it into the field.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its stellar companion.
articles.body: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to investigate the planet's missing water. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars. The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago. MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars . The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere.
